query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating an optimized amount of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into a high-entropy alloy (HEA) will significantly reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a broad temperature range by promoting the formation of a lubricious tribofilm and reinforcing the microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A self-lubricating high-entropy alloy (such as an AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA) produced without additional reinforcements and exhibiting higher friction and wear rates under sliding conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled volume fraction (~optimal around 30 wt.% based on prior studies) of WC particles into the HEA, for example via laser cladding, to form a composite coating with enhanced wear resistance.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under controlled loads and sliding speeds across a wide service temperature range (from room temperature up to approximately 800 °C) in ambient air.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a tribo-induced lubricious layer (tribofilm) that incorporates WC or its reaction products along with a refined microstructure, leading to enhanced hardness and stabilized protective oxide formation during sliding.
generation.mechanism: WC particles act by both reinforcing the HEA matrix—leading to solution strengthening and reduced plastic deformation—and by thermodynamically promoting a wear-induced reaction that forms a lubricious, protective nanolayer. This dual effect reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, lowering both friction and the wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA, the WC-enhanced HEA is predicted to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and a significantly reduced wear rate that remain stable over the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without WC reinforcement, which under similar sliding and temperature conditions shows relatively higher friction coefficients and wear rates.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under sliding wear conditions and temperatures up to around 800 °C, beyond which the stability of both the WC phase and the generated tribofilm may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal WC content for maximum effect and the long-term durability of the tribofilm under cyclic loading and varying environmental conditions require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group consisting of the baseline HEA and the other with an optimized WC particle reinforcement via laser cladding. Conduct ball‐on‐disk sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures (RT to 800 °C) and identical loads and sliding speeds. Compare the friction coefficients and wear rates between the two groups.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using in situ friction measurements
Wear volume and track depth via profilometry and microscopy
Microstructural analysis of the worn surfaces (e.g., SEM/EDX) to identify tribofilm formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC-reinforced HEA does not demonstrate a statistically significant decrease in both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across the temperature range relative to the untreated HEA, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Under the same dry friction conditions, the addition of an appropriate amount of WC particles can reduce the friction coefficient of the HEA matrix. In addition, the wear volume of the WC–HEA composite decreases rapidly with the increase of WC content. The wear volume of the 30 WC–HEA composite is 1.47 × 105 μm3, accounting for only 3.17% of the pure matrix material, indicating that the HEA with WC particles have better wear resistance.

Laser cladding, as an advanced method of coating preparation, can achieve metallurgical bonding between the coating material and substrate, which is important for the preparation of agricultural knives in harsh working conditions []. It has the characteristics of low dilution rate, high bonding strength, and fast solidification []. The short process time of preparing HEA by laser cladding can offset the shortcomings of the traditional methods. So, laser cladding was used in this study to prepare the HEA layer on silage knives. AlCoCrFeNi is a representative HEA system, which is considered as a kind of coating material that can be deposited on traditional alloys to improve their hardness and wear resistance []. The WC particles were added in the AlCoCrFeNi HEA, and then were coated on one side of the cutting edge of 65 Mn steel by laser cladding. The effect of WC on performance of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating was studied, and its microstructure, hardness and wear resistance were carefully analyzed in order to develop an alloy coating with high wear resistance.
